The minimal set of vertices output by MT.CoSet(I) has an elegant characterization: the vertices
in the copaths for I but not the paths for I. In fact, not by chance, this set of vertices
has appeared before in the context of the hiding property of Merkle commitment schemes in
Lemma 18.6.3.
Lemma 29.2.1. MT.CoSet(I) = copath(I)zpath(I).
Proof. The sets Ad , . . . , A0 consist of the vertices in path(I). Indeed, Ad is initialized with the
leaf vertices corresponding to the indices in I. Then, for j = d ´ 1, . . . , 1, 0, the algorithm sets
Aj to equal the parents of the vertices in Aj+1 . We conclude that YjPt0,1,...,du Aj = path(I).
   The output of the algorithm is B ‹ := YjP[d] Bj‹ . We argue that B ‹ = copath(I)zpath(I).
  • If a vertex is in YjPt0,1,...,du Aj = path(I) then the algorithm does not add the vertex to
     B‹.
  • If the algorithm adds a vertex to B ‹ then the vertex is the sibling of a vertex in
     YjPt0,1,...,du Aj = path(I), and hence the vertex is in copath(I).
  • Fix v P copath(I)zpath(I). If v is an odd vertex we can write v = (j + 1, 2i ´ 1) for
     j P t0, 1, . . . , d ´ 1u and i P [2j ], or else if v is an even vertex we can write v = (j + 1, 2i).
     Suppose without loss of generality that v is odd (the even case is similar). The sibling
     v 1 = (j + 1, 2i) of v is in Aj+1 Ď path(I), so in the (j, i)-th iteration of the algorithm the
     condition in Item 3b holds. Since v R path(I), we know that v R Aj+1 . Hence the algorithm
     adds v to Bj+1   ‹    Ď B‹.


  Path pruning requires modifying the algorithms MT.Open and MT.Check of the Merkle
commitment scheme in Section 18.1 to the constructions MT.Open‹ and MT.Check‹ below.
 • MT.Openf‹ (td, I) Ñ pf
       1. Compute the set of vertices B ‹ := MT.CoSet(I).
       2. Output the opening proof

                                 pf := (τi )iPI , (c(j,i) )(j,i)PMT.CoSet(I) .

     Namely, the opening proof pf includes the salts for all the authenticated leaves and the

                                          |I| ¨ s + |MT.CoSet(I)| ¨ σ .                            (29.3)
     If privacy is not desired then s = 0, in which case the size of pf is |MT.CoSet(I)| ¨ σ.
 • MT.Checkf‹ (rt, I, a, pf) Ñ b
       1. Parse pf as in Equation 29.2.
       2. For every i P I, compute the commitment c(d,i) := f (a[i], τi ).
       3. For j = d ´ 1, . . . , 0 (in this order) and i P [2j ]:
             if (j, i) P path(I) then set c(j,i) := f (c(j+1,2i´1) , c(j+1,2i) ) P t0, 1uσ .
       4. Check that rt = c(0,1) . (Note that (0, 1) P path(I).)
     The algorithm MT.Check‹ makes |path(I)| queries to the random oracle, and runs in time
     proportional to |copath(I) Y path(I)|.

Efficiency of path pruning The size of an opening proof pf with path pruning is |I| ¨ s +
|MT.CoSet(I)| ¨ σ (see Equation 29.3), compared to |I| ¨ s + |I| ¨ d ¨ σ without path pruning.
Therefore the effectiveness of path pruning is determined by the size of the set MT.CoSet(I).
   It is clear that |MT.CoSet(I)| ď |I| ¨ d. But how does |MT.CoSet(I)| behave?
   Intuitively, as the size of I increases so does the size of MT.CoSet(I). However when |I| = [`]
(all locations) then MT.CoSet(I) = H because there is no need to provide any commitments to
recover the Merkle commitment rt starting from all message entries and salt strings. Hence, as
I increases in size, the size of MT.CoSet(I) eventually decreases and becomes zero.
   In order to build intuition it is useful to discuss two extreme settings.

 • Good case. The good case is when the locations in I are all the leaves of a subtree of T`
   (in which case |I| is a power of 2). In this case, the commitment corresponding to the
   root vertex of the subtree can be deduced from the message entries and salt strings over
   I, without the need for any additional information. From thereon it suffices to provide
   commitments for vertices in the copath of the root vertex, and this copath consists of
   d ´ log2 |I| vertices. Overall in this case |MT.CoSet(I)| = d ´ log2 |I|.
    Figure 29.5 illustrates this phenomenon for message length ` = 16 and index set I =
    t1, 2, 3, 4u, in which case the tree depth is d = 4. The yellow leaf vertices are the
    opened locations and the blue vertices are those whose commitments are included in the
    opening proof. We see that the size of MT.CoSet(I) is 2, which agrees with the expression
    d ´ log2 |I| = 4 ´ log2 4 = 4 ´ 2 = 2.

 • Bad case. The bad case is when the locations in I are as spread out as possible, for
   example take the set I = tj ¨ |I|
                                  `
                                     ujP|I| (and assume that |I| divides `, in which case |I| is
    a power of 2). In this case each location is “alone” in a subtree of |I|
                                                                           `
                                                                              leaves; for each
    of these |I| subtrees, computing the commitment of the root vertex requires obtaining
    commitments corresponding to a copath of length log2 |I|
                                                           `
                                                             = log2 ` ´ log2 |I| = d ´ log2 |I|.
    Thereon, given the commitments of the root vertices of the |I| subtrees, one can compute
    the commitment of the root vertex of T` without any additional information. Overall in
    this case |MT.CoSet(I)| = |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|).
    Figure 29.6 illustrates this phenomenon for message length ` = 16 and index set I =
    t2, 7, 12, 14u, in which case the tree depth is d = 4. The yellow leaf vertices are the
    opened locations and the blue vertices are those whose commitments are included in the
    opening proof. We see that the size of MT.CoSet(I) is 8, which agrees with the expression
    |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|) = 4 ¨ (4 ´ log2 4) = 8.

The above examples represent extremal situations, as captured by the following lemma. The
upper bound in the lemma improves on the prior (trivial) upper bound |I| ¨ d.

Lemma 29.2.2. d ´ log2 |I| ď |MT.CoSet(I)| ď |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|).

Proof. We establish the lower bound and the upper bound separately.

Lower bound First we assume that |I| is a power of 2, and then show how to handle the
general case. The case where |I| is a power of 2 follows from the claim below, where we set
k := log2 |I|.
Claim 29.2.3. There exists a sequence of subsets I0 , . . . , Ik Ď [`] that satisfies the following.
29 Merkle commitment scheme optimizations                                                             332




 1. I0 = I and |I0 | = ¨ ¨ ¨ = |Ik |.
 2. For every j P t0, 1, . . . , k ´ 1u, |MT.CoSet(Ij+1 )| ď |MT.CoSet(Ij )|.
 3. |MT.CoSet(Ik )| = d ´ log2 |I|.
 4. For every j P t0, 1, . . . , ku and every subtree of T` with 2j leaf vertices, either no leaf vertex
    of the subtree is in Ij or all of the leaf vertices of the subtree are in Ij .

  The claim suffices because

                d ´ log2 |I| = |MT.CoSet(Ik )| ď |MT.CoSet(I0 )| = |MT.CoSet(I)| .

Proof of Claim 29.2.3. We define I0 := I and then recursively define the other subsets.
   Given Ij that satisfies the above properties (for index j), we initially set Ij+1 := Ij and then
modify Ij+1 so that it satisfies the above properties (for index j + 1).
   Suppose that there exists a subtree T of size 2j+1 whose leaf vertices partially overlap
with Ij+1 . (If no such subtree T exists, then we are done since Ij+1 satisfies all the required
properties.) Let TL be its left subtree and TR be its right subtree. Either no leaf vertex of TL is
in Ij+1 and all leaf vertices of TR are in Ij+1 , or vice versa (otherwise there would be a subtree
of size 2j whose leaf vertices partially overlap with Ij ). Moreover, if one such subtree T exists,
then another such subtree T 1 also exists (as |I| is a power of 2). Overall, there are subtrees T
and T 1 , with left and right subtrees for TL , TR (for T ) and TL1 , TR1 (for T 1 ). Moreover, assume
(without loss of generality) that all leaf vertices of TL and TL1 are in Ij+1 and no leaf vertices of
either TR or TR1 are in Ij+1 .
   We remove the leaf vertices of TL1 from Ij+1 and add to Ij+1 the leaf vertices of TR . This
ensures that no leaf vertex of T 1 is in Ij+1 , and all leaf vertices of T are in Ij+1 . Moreover, this
swap does not increase the size of MT.CoSet(Ij+1 ). The root vertex of TR is in MT.CoSet(Ij )
(in order to authenticate the leaf vertices of TL ). After adding the leaf vertices of TR to Ij+1 ,
this root vertex can be derived from the leaf vertices of TR , so it is not in MT.CoSet(Ij+1 ).
Since the leaves of TR1 were removed from Ij+1 , commitments of other vertices might be added
to MT.CoSet(Ij+1 ). The only vertex that might be added is the root vertex of TR1 . Overall, one
vertex has been removed and (at most) one is added, so |MT.CoSet(Ij+1 )| ď |MT.CoSet(Ij )|
(the size did not increase).
   We continue this process until no such subtrees exist. At the end, Ij+1 satisfies all properties.
   Finally, since 2k = |I| = |Ik |, Ik consists of all the leaf vertices of a subtree with 2k leaf
vertices, so, as discussed in the “good case” above the lemma, |MT.CoSet(Ik )| = d ´ log2 |Ik | =
d ´ log2 |I|.

  If |I| is not a power of 2, then we define a subset I 1 Ď I whose cardinality is a power of 2
such that |MT.CoSet(I)| ě |MT.CoSet(I 1 )|. We derive I 1 from I by removing indices as follows.
Initially set I 1 := I. If 2 does not divide |I 1 |, there exists a leaf vertex in I 1 whose sibling is not
in I 1 ; we remove this leaf vertex, which does not increase the size of MT.CoSet(I 1 ). Next, if 4
does not divide |I 1 |, there exists a pair of sibling leaf vertices in I 1 for which the children of
their parent’s sibling both are not in I 1 ; we remove this pair of siblings (which are leaf vertices),
which does not increase the size of MT.CoSet(I 1 ). This continues until |I 1 | is a power of 2.
  At the end of this process, we obtain I 1 for which we can apply the proved lower bound:

                  |MT.CoSet(I)| ě ˇMT.CoSet(I 1 )ˇ ě d ´ log2 ˇI 1 ˇ ě d ´ log2 |I| .
                                  ˇ              ˇ            ˇ ˇ
29 Merkle commitment scheme optimizations                                                         333




Upper bound First we assume that |I| is a power of 2, and then we discuss the general case.
   Again setting k := log2 |I|, we perform a sequence of swaps on I that do not decrease the
size of MT.CoSet(I). Suppose that there exists a subtree T with 2d´k leaf vertices with at least
two leaf vertices in I, denoted v1 , v2 . Then, there exists a subtree T 1 of the same size with no
leaf vertex in I (as otherwise the total number of elements in I would be larger than 2k = |I|).
We remove from I the index for v2 and add to I the index for an arbitrary leaf vertex v of T 1 .
Since T 1 had no leaf vertices in I, MT.CoSet(I) now contains d ´ k new vertices for the copath
of v. We removed v2 , and thus vertices from MT.CoSet(I) might be removed. However, since
v1 , v2 are both in T , at most d ´ k vertices are removed. Overall, the size of MT.CoSet(I) did
not decrease.
   We continue in this manner until all subtrees T with 2d´k leaves have exactly one leaf in I.
At this point, the size of MT.CoSet(I) is upper bounded by |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|) as discussed in
the “bad case” above the lemma.
   If |I| is not a power of 2, then let K be the smallest power of two with K ě |I|. As explained
in the “bad case” above, each location of I is “alone” in a subtree of K` leaves. Thus, each
copath has size d ´ log2 K, and subtrees that do not have a leaf in I (there are K ´ |I| such
subtrees) cause their root vertex to be in MT.CoSet(I). Overall, we get the bound

                 |MT.CoSet(I)| = |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 K) + (K ´ |I|)
                                                                 
                                                              K
                               = |I| ¨ d ´ log2 |I| ´ log2          + (K ´ |I|)
                                                              |I|

                               ě |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|) ´ |I| ¨ 0
                                 = |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|) .

Above, the inequality holds since the function log2 (x) ´ x + 1 is non-negative for x P (1, 2).

   The upper bound |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|) is a concave function of q := |I| over the interval
t0, 1, . . . , `u: it equals 0 when q = 0 or q = ` = 2d (the two endpoints of the interval); and in
between the function increases as q increases up to some threshold q0 and after that decreases.
The threshold is where the derivative d ´ log2 e ´ log2 q of q ¨ (d ´ log2 q) vanishes. Hence
the (non-integer) threshold is q0 := 2e = e` . Since e « 2.72, we know that q0 P [2d´2 , 2d´1 ].

This computation provides an indication for the location of the threshold for |MT.CoSet(I)|,
provided I is sufficiently spread out (in which case |MT.CoSet(I)| is close to its upper bound
|I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|)).

Concrete efficiency In typical scenarios the set I is the result of sampling locations from
some high-entropy distribution, so I is likely to be reasonably spread out. In these cases we
expect |MT.CoSet(I)| to be closer to the upper bound |I| ¨ (d ´ log2 |I|) rather than the lower
bound d ´ log2 |I|. We illustrate this phenomenon via some empirical data.
  We perform the following experiment. Consider the Merkle commitment scheme applied to

σ = 256, and the salt size is s = 128. We consider a random subset I of [`] = [220 ] of size q for
progressively larger values: we consider q P t2i uiPt0,1,...,20u . Note that q = 20 = 1 corresponds to

 • Salts contribute g0 := |I| ¨ s = q ¨ s bits to the opening proof. These bits must be included

29.2.3 Security

Path pruning required changing the algorithms MT.Open and MT.Check into corresponding
variants MT.Open‹ and MT.Check‹ . Here we discuss how these modifications do not impact
the security properties of the Merkle commitment scheme that we proved in Chapter 18.
29 Merkle commitment scheme optimizations                                                      336




Compressing and expanding opening proofs The path pruning optimization can be viewed as
compressing an “uncompressed” opening proof and, conversely, the path pruning optimization
can be undone by expanding a compressed opening proof. We use this structure further below
to discuss the security of path pruning.

 • Compression. The algorithm MT.Openf‹ (td, I) outputs an opening proof pf‹ that includes
   the salt strings for locations in I and the commitments corresponding to vertices in
   MT.CoSet(I). Since MT.CoSet(I) Ď copath(I) (see Lemma 29.2.1), the “compressed”
   opening proof pf‹ can be derived from an “uncompressed” opening proof pf output by
   MT.Openf (td, I) by omitting the commitments corresponding to vertices that are not in
   MT.CoSet(I) (without knowing the opening trapdoor td).
    In more detail, define MT.Compress to be the function that omits redundant commitments.
        MT.Compress(pf, I):
          1. Parse pf as (authi )iPI , and each authi as τi , (cv )vPcopath(i) .
                                                                              

          2. Compute B ‹ := MT.CoSet(I). 
          3. Output the opening proof pf‹ := (τi )iPI , (c(j,i) )(j,i)PMT.CoSet(I) .
                                                                                  

    The output of MT.Compress agrees with the output of MT.Open‹ :

                      MT.Openf‹ (td, I) = MT.Compress(MT.Openf (td, I), I) .

 • Expansion. The path pruning optimization can be undone: given query access to the
   random oracle, an opening proof pf‹ in the path-pruning format can be expanded into
   an opening proof pf that is a list of authentication paths. This is not surprising because
   path pruning removes redundancy without any information loss, so the redundancy can be
   added back.
    In more detail, define MT.Expand to be the function that adds missing commitments.
        MT.Expandf (pf‹ , I):
         1. Parse pf‹ as (τi )iPI , (c(j,i) )(j,i)PMT.CoSet(I) .
                                                             

         2. For every i P I, compute the commitment c(d,i) := f (a[i], τi ).
         3. For j = d ´ 1, . . . , 0 (in this order) and i P [2j ]:
               if (j, i) P path(I) then set c(j,i) := f (c(j+1,2i´1) , c(j+1,2i)
                                                                               ) P t0, 1u .
                                                                                          σ

         4. Output pf := (authi )iPI , where authi := τi , (cv )vPcopath(i) .
    Note that the algorithm has all the commitments needed for the authentication paths
    because the algorithm computes the commitments corresponding to vertices in path(I) and
    copath(I)zMT.CoSet(I) Ď path(I) (see Lemma 29.2.1).
    Expanding a compressed opening proof recovers the starting opening proof:

                              MT.Expandf (MT.Compress(pf, I), I) = pf .

    In particular, the expanded proof is equivalent to the compressed proof in the following
    sense:

             MT.Checkf‹ (rt, I, a, pf‹ ) = MT.Checkf (rt, I, a, MT.Expandf (pf‹ , I)) , and
             MT.Checkf (rt, I, a, pf) = MT.Checkf‹ (rt, I, a, MT.Compress(pf, I)) .
29 Merkle commitment scheme optimizations                                                          337




    Moreover, the query-answer trace S‹ of MT.Check‹ and the query-answer trace S of
    MT.Check are equal (up to the order of query-answer pairs). Specifically, in each case the
    query-answer trace contains the following |path(I)| entries:
      – for every i P I, the query (a[i], τi ) yielding the answer c(d,i) := f (m[i], τi );
      – for every (j, i) P YiPI path(i)zt(d, i)u, the query (c(j+1,2i´1) , c(j+1,2i) ) yielding the
        answer c(j,i) := f (c(j+1,2i´1) , c(j+1,2i) ).

Properties Since the path-pruning optimization can be viewed as compressing opening proofs
and these can be expanded to recover the starting opening proofs, there is a correspondence
between adversaries against the Merkle commitment scheme without or with path pruning.
The correspondence has a (small) cost, because MT.Expand queries the random oracle. This
means that the query bound of adversaries may increase by a small additive factor that equals
the size of the query-trace of MT.Expand. However this cost can be avoided by inspecting the
proof of each of the security properties of interest to us.

 • Collision lemma. Lemma 18.3.2 and its special case Lemma 18.3.1 hold as stated for
   the Merkle commitment scheme with path pruning, that is, with MT.Check‹ instead of
   MT.Check. Indeed, for every b P t0, 1u, we have that MT.Checkf‹ (rt, Ib , ab , pfb ) equals
   MT.Checkf (rt, Ib , ab , MT.Expandf (pfb , I)), and the query-answer traces of both executions
   are equal when viewed as sets.

 • Binding. Lemma 18.4.1 holds as stated for the Merkle commitment scheme with path
   pruning, that is, with MT.Check‹ instead of MT.Check. The analysis carries over with
   minimal changes. Each appearance of MT.Check is replaced with MT.Check‹ . Next, the
   analysis of the event E ^ Ecol refers to authentication paths for single locations, which do
   not exist in an opening proof in path-pruning format; instead, one refers to authentication
   paths in the expanded opening proof. In more detail, for every b P t0, 1u, authb is the
   authentication path for location i in MT.Expandf (pfb , I); then MT.Checkf‹ (rt, Ib , ab , pfb ) = 1
   implies that MT.Checkf (rt, i, ab [i], authb ) = 1. Finally, one relies on the collision lemma for
   MT.Check (even though the statement is about MT.Check‹ ).

 • Extractability. Lemma 18.5.1 (single extraction), Lemma 18.5.7 (multi-extraction), and
   Lemma 18.5.10 (multi-extraction across multiple configurations) hold as stated for the
   Merkle commitment scheme with path pruning, that is, with MT.Check‹ and MT.Open‹
   instead of MT.Check and MT.Open. The extractor MT.Extract in Construction 18.5.3
   remains the same. The analyses of the lemmas carry over with minimal changes. We

   similar.
    Each appearance of MT.Check is replaced with MT.Check‹ , and similarly each ˇappearance

 • Hiding. We discuss separately the two hiding lemmas.
    Lemma 18.6.1 only involves the commitment algorithm MT.Commit, which is unaffected

    Lemma 18.6.3 additionally involves the opening algorithm MT.Open, which is replaced by

30 Special soundness
Special soundness is a knowledge soundness property satisfied by many sigma protocols (SPs) and
public-coin interactive proofs (IPs) of interest (see Chapter 27). Informally, special soundness
states that there exists an efficient knowledge extractor that finds a valid witness, for a given
instance, when provided with a suitable “tree” of accepting interaction transcripts of the proof
system. Such trees can then be produced from any prover that is sufficiently convincing, by
rerunning the prover multiple times on suitably correlated inputs.1
   A crucial implication, from the perspective of this book, is that special soundness implies
(rewinding) state-restoration knowledge soundness. In turn, this means that: (i) SPs that have
special soundness yield non-interactive arguments that have (adaptive and rewinding) knowledge
soundness via the Fiat–Shamir transformation for SPs (discussed in Part II); and (ii) public-
coin IPs that have special soundness yield non-interactive arguments that have (adaptive
and rewinding) knowledge soundness via the Fiat–Shamir transformation for public-coin IPs
(discussed in Part III).
   In this chapter we discuss definitions of special soundness and establish the implication to
rewinding state-restoration knowledge soundness.2

Organization In Section 30.1 we define special soundness for SPs and public-coin IPs. First,
we study special soundness for SPs: in Section 30.2 we show that it implies (standard) rewinding
knowledge soundness; then in Section 30.3 we show that it implies state-restoration rewinding
knowledge soundness. Second, we study special soundness for public-coin IPs: in Section 30.4
we show that it implies (standard) rewinding knowledge soundness; then in Section 30.5 we
show that it implies state-restoration rewinding knowledge soundness.

Remark 30.0.1 (extraction tradeoffs). All results in this chapter achieve a notion of rewinding
knowledge soundness that is slightly stronger than the general definitions used earlier in this
book: the knowledge soundness error does not depend on the failure probability of the adversary.
Informally, this is because the rewinding knowledge extractor runs in expected time until it
succeeds and, as long as the adversary convinces the verifier with high enough probability,
the rewinding knowledge extractor will succeed. However this is merely a point in a tradeoff
space. All extractors in this chapter could be modified to run in less time at the cost of a larger
knowledge soundness error. Intuitively, the extractor will give up after some number of rewinds,
and the larger the adversary’s failure probability then the larger the knowledge soundness error.
Analyses for such knowledge extractors (which we do not include in this book) would result in
a knowledge soundness error that depends on the adversary’s failure probability.
 1
   The term special soundness is historical and, unfortunately, uninformative. The property is a strengthening
    of knowledge soundness rather than soundness, and involves extractors that rewind the prover to construct
    certain trees of accepting interaction transcripts. A term such as tree-based knowledge soundness would be more
    appropriate, but we avoid it for the sake of historical consistency.
 2
   All definitions and results about special soundness for public-coin IPs naturally extend to the case of special
    soundness for public-coin IOPs (which can sometimes be of interest).
30 Special soundness                                                                               340




30.1 Extraction from forks and trees
We define the notion of special soundness for SPs and then for public-coin IPs.

The case of SPs An SP is a 3-message protocol between a prover and a verifier (see Chapter 8).
An SP has special soundness if a witness can be efficiently deduced from a fork of accepting
interaction transcripts for the given instance. A fork consists of multiple accepting interaction
transcripts that share the same SP prover commitment and have pairwise distinct SP verifier
challenges. (The SP prover responses need not be distinct.) The number of transcripts of the
fork is determined by an arity parameter a P N. See Figure 30.1 for a diagram.

The case of public-coin IPs An IP is a multi-round protocol between a prover and a verifier
(see Chapter 13). A public-coin IP has special soundness if a witness can be efficiently deduced
from a tree of accepting interaction transcripts for the given instance. This latter consists of a
tree where vertices are labeled with IP prover messages, edges are labeled IP verifier messages,
and every path from the root to a leaf is an accepting transcript; edges sharing the same vertex
are labeled with pairwise distinct IP verifier messages. A list of parameters a1 , . . . , ak P N
determines the number of children that each vertex in the tree has, depending on the layer. See
Figure 30.2 for a diagram.

special soundness increases; neither depends on the failure probability of the SP prover.

for x.3 Informally, SRForkFinder identifies the first move (if any) corresponding to (x, α1 , σ),
and then reruns P̃sr     SP with freshly sampled answers (consistently answering other moves as
needed) until enough accepting SP interaction transcripts with the same instance and SP prover
message are found. Intuitively, this takes a multiplicative factor (t + 1) more reruns compared
to Lemma 30.2.2, as P̃sr    SP makes at most t moves and can also output something corresponding
to no move. Analyzing the success probability and expected running time of SRForkFinder is
more technical, and the simpler analysis for Lemma 30.2.2 is a useful warmup.

                                                 SP ):

          1. If VSP (x, α1 , ρ, α2 ) = 0 or |x|R ą n, abort.
          2. If the move-response pair ((x, α1 , σ), ρ) is not in trsr then append it to trsr .
          3. Lazily sample an oracle rṅd Ð U(R) that is consistent with the move-response trace
             trsr . (Lazily sample an oracle rṅd1 Ð U(R) and program the oracle rṅd := rṅd1 [trsr ].)
          4. Set S := Rztρu and B := t(ρ, α2 )u.

               b) Set µ := t((x, α1 , σ), ρ1 )u.

                                                                                        SP (s, rṅd[µ], P̃SP ).

Running time We analyze the expected running time of SRForkFinder. First we analyze how
SRForkFinder invokes P̃sr
                        SP . The algorithm SRForkFinder, in each iteration of the while loop,
simulates an execution of the SP state-restoration game with P̃sr SP (see Item 5c). In expectation
this happens E[X] ď (t + 1) ¨ (a ´ 1) times. Overall, since τP̃sr denotes the total running time
                                                                                    SP
of P̃sr
     SP (i.e., the running time within an execution of the SP state-restoration game), the total
time spent by SRForkFinder invoking P̃sr SP is upper bounded by (t + 1) ¨ (a ´ 1) ¨ τP̃sr . All other
                                                                                       SP
operations in SRForkFinder take time poly(len(x)), which in expectation across all while loop
iterations add up to time (t + 1) ¨ (a ´ 1) ¨ poly(len(x)).

30.4 Knowledge soundness for IPs
We prove that if an IP has special soundness then the IP has rewinding knowledge soundness.
The rewinding knowledge soundness error and extraction time increase as the arity of the
special soundness increases; neither depends on the failure probability of the IP prover.

Theorem 30.4.1. Let IP = (PIP , VIP ) be a public-coin IP with round complexity k. If IP has

IP has rewinding knowledge soundness error κIP with extraction time etIP (see Definition 13.1.5)

   Fix an instance x and IP prover P̃IP . The main idea to prove the theorem is to rewind P̃IP

   The lemma below provides a probabilistic procedure TreeFinder that outputs an (a1 , . . . , ak )-

((αi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ) between the IP prover P̃IP and IP verifier VIP , and black-box access to P̃IP .
We describe how to upper bound the probability that P̃IP convinces VIP and the output of
TreeFinder is not an (a1 , . . . , ak )-tree Tśfor x. Informally, TreeFinder invokes P̃IP with different
IP verifier challenges until it obtains iP[k] ai ´ 1 additional accepting interaction transcripts.
(The first accepting interaction transcript comes “for free” when the IP verifier VIP accepts in
the real interaction.)

Moreover, TreeFinder runs in expected time ( iP[k] ai ´ 1) ¨ (τP̃IP + poly(len(x))).
                                            ś

   The algorithm TreeFinder is the base case of a recursively defined helper function TreeFinderj ,
whose goal is to find, given an instance x and partial transcript ((αi1 )ji=1 , (ρ1i )ji=1 ), an (aj+1 , . . . , ak )-
subtree of (accepting) transcripts for the instance x and partial transcript ((αi1 )ji=1 , (ρ1i )ji=1 ).
The base case invoked by TreeFinder thus corresponds to j = 0.
   In more detail, TreeFinderj invokes TreeFinderj+1 multiple times, each time with a different IP
verifier message ρ1j+1 , until TreeFinderj obtains aj+1 subtrees for different IP verifier messages
(or else TreeFinderj outputs the error message fail). Then TreeFinderj combines these subtrees
to obtain the desired (aj+1 , . . . , ak )-subtree. Two delicate technical details complicate the
strategy.
  • Early abort. If the first invocation of TreeFinderj+1 by TreeFinderj results in a failure
    message (no valid subtree is returned) then TreeFinderj immediately halts and outputs
    a failure message. (Without making any further attempts.) This early abort condition
    ensures, as will be shown in the analysis, that the expected running time of TreeFinderj is
    suitably bounded.

  • Real transcript. The algorithm TreeFinderj additionally receives as input a complete
    interaction transcript ((αi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ) that corresponds to the “real” interaction between
    the IP prover P̃IP and IP verifier VIP . One (and only one) of the paths in the tree output by
    TreeFinderj (if not a failure message) corresponds to ((αi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ), which can be viewed
    as a “free” path (provided ((αi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ) is accepting). To accommodate for this, the
    left-most path of the tree is arbitrarily reserved for ((αi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ), which TreeFinderj
    realizes by receiving a flag f that is set when on the left-most branch. Specifically, if
    f = 1 then TreeFinderj makes the first invocation of TreeFinderj+1 with ρj+1 (and all other
    invocations of TreeFinderj+1 with f = 0 and different random strings in Rj+1 ). Instead, if
    f = 0 then TreeFinderj ignores ((αi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ), and all invocations of TreeFinderj+1 are
    with different random strings in Rj+1 .
The above summary is made precise in the construction below.

30.4.1 Technical details
In the proof of Lemma 30.4.2 we relied on two main claims: Claim 30.4.15 (bound on the error
probability) and Claim 30.4.18 (bound on the expected running time). The goal of this section
is to prove these claims; in each case, this requires additional notation and intermediate claims.

Preliminaries     We establish basic claims and notation for the analysis.

Claim 30.4.5. The following two random variables are identical:
     !                                                          ˇ                                   )

Proof. The equality holds because: (a) on the right side of the equality, TreeFinder0 with flag

replacement fresh SP verifier random messages for other recursive calls); (c) the SP verifier
messages (ρi )iP[k] are sampled at random.

30.5 State-restoration knowledge soundness for IPs
We prove that if a public-coin IP has special soundness then the IP has rewinding state-
restoration knowledge soundness. The rewinding state-restoration knowledge soundness error
and extraction time increase as the arity of the special soundness increases; neither depends on
the failure probability of the state-restoration IP prover.

   The proof of this theorem is similar to the proof of Theorem 30.4.1: rewind the given IP state-
restoration prover P̃sr  IP several times with correlated inputs in order to obtain an (a1 , . . . , ak )-tree
T for x; this suffices because the knowledge extractor Ess               IP for special soundness can find a
witness w from x and T . However, there are notable differences that make the proof more
technical. First, in rewinding state-restoration knowledge soundness (Definition 13.2.5), the IP
state-restoration prover P̃sr   IP chooses the instance x in the IP state-restoration game; in contrast,
in rewinding knowledge soundness (Definition 13.1.5) the instance x is fixed. Moreover, the
IP state-restoration prover P̃sr        IP can make multiple attempts at convincing the IP verifier, not
only with different instances but also with different IP partial transcripts; this complicates the
rewinding strategy.
   The lemma below provides a probabilistic procedure SRTreeFinder that outputs an (a1 , . . . , ak )-
tree T , which is analogous to Lemma 30.4.2. The procedure SRTreeFinder receives as input the
output (x, (αi )iP[k] , (σi )iP[k] , (ρi )iP[k] ) of the IP state-restoration game played by P̃sr
                                                                                                IP , the list of
                             sr        sr                                sr
move-response pairs tr of P̃IP , and black-box access to P̃IP . The main challenge is that each
time SRTreeFinder reruns P̃sr         IP we get a new output whose instance may not agree with that
received as input, which would not contribute progress towards the desired (a1 , . . . , ak )-tree
for x.4 Informally, SRTreeFinder identifies the first move (if any) corresponding to (x, α1 , σ),
and then reruns P̃sr    IP with freshly sampled answers (consistently answering other moves as
needed) until enough accepting IP interaction transcripts with the same instance and IP prover
message are found. Intuitively, this takes a multiplicative factor (t + 1) more reruns compared
to Lemma 30.4.2, as P̃sr     IP makes at most t moves and can also output something corresponding
to no move. Analyzing the success probability and expected running time of SRTreeFinder is
technical, and the simpler analysis for Lemma 30.4.2 serves as a useful warmup.

    SRTreeFinderj sets to 1 for the first invocation of SRTreeFinderj+1 and sets to 0 for the
    other invocations (if there is no early abort).

30.5.1 Technical details
In the proof of Lemma 30.5.2 we relied on two main claims: Claim 30.5.17 (bound on error
probability) and Claim 30.5.29 (bound on expected running time). The goal of this section
is to prove these claims; in each case, this requires introducing more notation and proving
intermediate claims.
   Below, for every j P t0, . . . , ku, we let Zj denote the set of random strings for SRTreeFinderj .

Error probability Here we focus on proving Claim 30.5.17. The algorithm SRTreeFinder
outputs an (a1 , . . . , ak )-tree T for x if and only if the tree T output by SRTreeFinder0 (invoked
in Item 3 of SRTreeFinder) is an (a1 , . . . , ak )-tree for x. The analysis focuses on upper bounding
the error probability of SRTreeFinder0 ; more generally, the analysis focuses on SRTreeFinderj
for j P t0, 1, . . . , ku.
   The algorithm SRTreeFinderj , when invoked with flag c = 1, receives the IP state-restoration
prover P̃sr
          IP and (lazily sampled) random oracle, and no other inputs (they are set to H instead).

31 Round-by-round soundness
Round-by-round soundness (and knowledge soundness) is a property that implies state-
restoration soundness (and knowledge soundness), and is satisfied by public-coin IPs and
public-coin IOPs of practical interest (see Chapter 27). In particular, a public-coin IP with
round-by-round soundness is suitable for use by the Fiat–Shamir transformation (Construc-
tion 14.1.1 or Construction 15.1.1), and a public-coin IOP with round-by-round soundness is
suitable for use by the BCS transformation (Construction 25.1.1). Round-by-round soundness
(and knowledge soundness) are attractive notions because they are relatively straightforward to
define, and it can be easier to establish that a given protocol satisfies them, in comparison to
establishing state-restoration soundness (and knowledge soundness).
   The material in this chapter is written for public-coin IOPs, and corresponding statements
hold for public-coin IPs (which are the special case where the verifier reads the prover’s messages
in their entirety).


Organization In Section 31.1 we define the notions of round-by-round soundness and round-
by-round knowledge soundness. In Section 31.2 we show how round-by-round soundness implies
state-restoration soundness. In Section 31.3 we show how round-by-round knowledge soundness
implies state-restoration knowledge soundness.


31.1 Definition
An IOP (in particular, IP) with round-by-round soundness is such that we can assign a bad
event to each round of the protocol, and when that bad event happens then the interaction
is “doomed” in that the malicious prover may have a way to win. Each round’s bad event is
upper bounded by a corresponding error.


State function The definition of round-by-round soundness relies on the notion of a state
function for a (possibly partial) transcript of interaction. Informally, the state function receives
as input an instance x and a (possibly partial) transcript trc, and outputs a bit denoting
whether the transcript is doomed. An empty transcript is not doomed; IOP prover messages
cannot make a transcript doomed; and a full transcript that is doomed is rejected by the IOP
verifier.

Definition 31.1.1. A state function for an IOP IOP = (PIOP , VIOP ) is a deterministic
(possibly inefficient) function RBRState that receives as input an instance x and an interaction
transcript trc and outputs a bit for which the following holds.
  • Empty transcript: if trc = H is the empty transcript then RBRState(x, trc) = 0.
  • Prover moves: if trc = (Π1 , ρ1 , . . . , Πi , ρi ) is a transcript for i rounds (for i ă k) with
                                                                      li+1
     RBRState(x, trc) = 0 then, for every IOP string Πi+1 P Σi+1           , RBRState(x, trc}Πi+1 ) = 0.
31 Round-by-round soundness                                                                               383




 • Full transcript: if trc = (Π1 , ρ1 , . . . , Πk , ρk ) is a full transcript and RBRState(x, trc) = 0
             (Πi )
     then VIOP iP[k] (x, (ρi )iP[k] ) = 0.

RBR soundness Round-by-round soundness states that, for every partial transcript where the
IOP verifier is about to move (to send randomness), if the instance is not in the language and
the transcript is not doomed, then the probability that the next random message of the IOP
verifier makes the transcript doomed is upper bounded by an error. Different rounds may have
different errors bounding this event, or one can consider a single error bounding all of them.
Definition 31.1.2. An IOP IOP = (PIOP , VIOP ) for a relation R has round-by-round
soundness errors (rbrIOP,i )iP[k] if there exists a state function RBRState such that for every

that is not doomed becomes doomed with probability above a certain threshold then an extractor
can efficiently find the witness from this transcript (and, indeed, any continuation of it). More
precisely, the extractor only needs the IOP strings sent by the prover in the transcript.

31.2 RBR soundness implies SR soundness
The theorem below states that the state-restoration soundness error of a public-coin IOP with
round complexity k is at most a multiplicative factor of t + k larger than its round-by-round
soundness error.
31 Round-by-round soundness                                                                                        388




Theorem 31.2.1. Let IOP = (PIOP , VIOP ) be a public-coin IOP. If IOP has round-by-round

31.3 RBR knowledge soundness implies SR knowledge soundness
The theorem below about knowledge soundness is analogous to Theorem 31.2.1 (which is about
soundness): it states that the state-restoration knowledge soundness error of a public-coin IOP
with round complexity k is at most a multiplicative factor of t + k larger than its round-by-round
knowledge soundness error.

32 Argument systems with preprocessing
We describe preprocessing argument systems, an offline-online model for argument systems that
can be used to achieve succinct verification even for computations whose description is large.
Such argument systems are constructed from holographic probabilistic proofs, via an extension
of transformations studied in this book that relies on the Merkle commitment scheme. This
extension is known as the Chiesa–Ojha–Spooner (COS) transformation [COS20]. In this chapter
we introduce the new notions of preprocessing and holography, and explain how holographic
probabilistic proofs lead to preprocessing succinct arguments.


Organization We start with informal discussions:
  • in Section 32.1 we sketch the preprocessing setting for argument systems;
  • in Section 32.2 we sketch the holographic setting for probabilistic proof systems; and
  • in Section 32.3 we sketch how holography leads to preprocessing.
These informal discussions do not focus on any specific type of probabilistic proof (whether an
SP, IP, PCP, or IOP) nor focus on the type of argument (interactive or non-interactive), since
the notions and ideas apply to all of these settings. A formal treatment, however, necessitates
being concrete, so in the remaining sections we focus on transforming a holographic IOP (the
most general type of probabilistic proof considered in this book) to a preprocessing NARG
(harder than constructing a preprocessing IARG). We proceed as follows:
  • in Section 32.4 we define preprocessing NARGs;
  • in Section 32.5 we define holographic IOPs;
  • in Section 32.6 we provide state-restoration definitions for holographic IOPs;
  • in Section 32.7 we describe the COS transformation, which extends the BCS transformation
     (which transforms a public-coin IOP to a NARG) to the holography-to-preprocessing setting;
  • in Section 32.8 we discuss the security properties of the COS transformation.
In these sections, we consider notions that are delicate extensions of notions introduced in prior
chapters. Opting for a comprehensive treatment, we provide complete definitions for these new
notions. This necessarily expands discussions, but avoids ambiguities that would arise if we
only outlined the new notions by describing differences from the prior ones.


32.1 The preprocessing setting
The argument verifier V of an argument system receives as input the instance x and, in
particular, its running time tV is at least len(x), because merely reading the input x takes
time len(x). This is undesirable when x is large (e.g., x is the binary representation of a large
arbitrary circuit). How can the argument verifier V run in time that is much less than len(x)?
   The preprocessing setting is an offline-online model intended to accommodate an expensive
offline phase followed by a cheap online phase. We elaborate on this below.
32 Argument systems with preprocessing                                                                      396




Indexed relations and languages The starting point is splitting an instance x into two pieces:
a “large” index i for the offline phase and a “small” instance x for the online phase. This split
necessitates extending the notions of a relation and language to accommodate for the fact that
a full instance consists of a pair (i, x) where i is the index and x is the instance.

Definition 32.1.1. An indexed relation Ri is a set consisting of index-instance-witness
triples (i, x, w). The corresponding indexed language L(Ri ) is the set of index-instance pairs
(i, x) for which there exists a witness w such that (i, x, w) is in the indexed relation Ri .

  The terminology “indexed” comes from the fact that an indexed relation Ri can be viewed
as a collection of (standard) relations (Ri )i where Ri := t(x, w) : (i, x, w) P Ri u and, similarly,
an indexed language L can also be viewed as a collection of (standard) languages (Li )i where
Li := tx : (i, x) P Lu. Thus i plays the role of an index to elements in the collection.
  We give an example of an indexed relation based on the satisfiability of boolean formulas.
The indexed relation RSATi   consists of triples (i, x, w) where i describes a SAT formula φ, and
the instance x and witness w are binary strings such that x}w is a satisfying assignment for φ.
The large part of the full instance is the SAT formula, and the small part of the full instance is
a partial variable assignment; the witness is an assignment to the remaining variables.

Argument systems with preprocessing We outline how an (interactive or non-interactive)
argument system works in the preprocessing setting.

 • Offline phase: indexer algorithm. A preprocessing argument system involves an
   additional algorithm I, known as the argument indexer. In the offline phase, I receives
   as input an index i (and query access to the random oracle) and outputs two index keys,
   a prover index key pik and a verifier index key vik. This offline phase, where the index i
   is preprocessed to obtain corresponding index keys, is intended to be “trusted” in that
   security properties of the preprocessing argument system are intended to hold for honestly
   generated index keys. The index keys are considered public information, so adversaries in
   security definitions receive index keys as input.1
        The index algorithm is required to be deterministic in order to reduce the need to trust
        this offline phase. In such a case, anyone can rerun the index algorithm and confirm the
        correctness of the resulting index keys. See Remark 32.4.8 for a discussion about this.

 • Online phase: prover and verifier algorithms. In a standard (non-preprocessing)
   argument system the argument prover P receives as input an instance x and witness w
   and the argument verifier V receives as input an instance x. (Moreover, they both receive
   query access to the random oracle.) In the preprocessing setting, the argument prover
   P additionally receives as input the prover index key pik and the argument verifier V
   additionally receives as input the verifier index key vik.
        The running time of the argument verifier V is at least len(vik) + len(x) (as V receives as
        input vik and x), and typically is at most poly(len(vik), len(x)). This enables V, in principle,
        to run in time that is much less than len(i) + len(x) (the length of the full instance (i, x)),
        because vik is typically much shorter than i. Intuitively, the argument indexer I relies on
        the random oracle to produce a short commitment vik to the long index i.
 1
     This is in contrast to adversaries receiving only the prover index key, which would correspond to a private-
      verification relaxation of a preprocessing argument, a notion that we do not consider in this book.
             32 Argument systems with preprocessing                                                           397

             argument (IARG) and a preprocessing non-interactive argument (NARG). In Section 32.4 we
             provide a formal treatment of preprocessing NARGs.

             In Section 32.1 we motivated and outlined the preprocessing setting, an offline-online model

             offline-online model analogously defined for probabilistic proof systems.
                Similarly to preprocessing argument systems, holographic probabilistic proofs: (a) consider
             relations and languages that are indexed (see Definition 32.1.1), and (b) additionally involve an
             indexer algorithm I. The offline phase and online phase work as follows.

              • Offline phase. The indexer I is a deterministic algorithm that receives as input an index i
                and outputs two “encoded indices”, a prover encoded index ip and a verifier encoded index
                iv . Hence, the offline phase consists of the computation (ip , iv ) := I(i). Note that the offline
                phase depends solely on the index i and, in particular, the same encoded indices can be
                used for different instances x and witnesses w (which are unknown until the online phase).

              • Online phase. Recall that in a (non-holographic) probabilistic proof the prover receives as
                input an instance x and a witness w and the verifier receives as input the instance x. In a
                holographic probabilistic proof, the prover and verifier additionally receive information
                from the offline phase: the prover additionally receives as input the prover encoded index
                ip and the verifier additionally receives query access to the verifier encoded index iv . In
                particular, the verifier encoded index iv is an oracle intended to enable the verifier to check
                statements about the index i without receiving the index i (or iv ) as an explicit input.
                The prover and verifier interact according to whichever type of probabilistic proof one is
                considering, and the verifier eventually outputs a decision bit.

                32.3 From holography to preprocessing
           𝕚    𝕚𝕩

                We informally explain how any holographic probabilistic proof system naturally leads to a
                preprocessing argument system in the ROM. The idea underlying this implication is intuitive
                and flexible: every transformation studied in this book can be extended to support holography-
                to-preprocessing, and similar extensions hold in other settings (e.g., beyond the pure ROM).
                Later, in Section 32.7 we provide a detailed description of this idea for the case of preprocessing
                NARGs constructed from holographic IOPs, which is known as the COS transformation.
                 2
                     This is analogous to how, in a preprocessing argument, the argument verifier receives as input the correct verifier
                      index key, regardless of what a malicious argument prover may do.
32 Argument systems with preprocessing                                                                             399




The argument indexer We describe how to construct, in the ROM, an argument indexer I
starting from a given indexer I for an underlying probabilistic proof (SP, IP, PCP, IOP). The
argument indexer I, given an index i and access to a random oracle (or random oracles), is
tasked with producing a prover index key pik and a verifier index key vik that can be used,
respectively, by the argument prover P and argument verifier V in the online phase later on.
First I runs I, obtaining encoded indices ip and iv for the prover and verifier respectively. The
verifier of the probabilistic proof will want to query iv ; to facilitate this, I commits to iv via the
Merkle commitment scheme using a random oracle fMT0 , resulting in a Merkle commitment rt0
(to include in vik) and trapdoor td0 . As no hiding properties are needed, the Merkle commitment
scheme is configured without salts (the salt size is set to zero). Moreover, the argument verifier
V may need to hash the “full instance” (i, x); to facilitate this, I uses a random oracle f0 to
hash the index to obtain ρ0 := f0 (i) to include in vik, so that the argument verifier V may hash
(ρ0 , x) instead of (i, x). The prover index pik is set to (ip , iv , td0 , ρ0 ) and the verifier index key
vik is set to (rt0 , ρ0 ).
   The above strategy is summarized in the construction of the argument indexer below, and
essentially remains the same no matter the online phase or probabilistic proof.

Construction 32.3.1. Let I be the indexer of the probabilistic proof, which receives as input
an index i and outputs a prover encoded index ip and verifier encoded index iv ; let alphabet Σ0
be the alphabet of iv and l0 the length of iv (over this alphabet). Define MT0 := MT[λ, Σ0 , l0 , 0]
to be the Merkle commitment scheme for random oracle output size λ, messages over alphabet
Σ0 of length l0 , and salt size 0 (no hiding properties). We describe an argument indexer I,
which receives as input an index i and query access to random oracles (fMT0 , f0 ) P Ub (λ)2 , and
outputs a prover index key pik and verifier index key vik.

        I (fMT0 ,f0 ) (i):
          1. Compute a hash of the index: ρ0 := f0 (i) P t0, 1uλ .3
          2. Compute the prover encoded index and verifier encoded index: (ip , iv ) := I(i).
          3. Commit to iv via the Merkle commitment scheme MT0 :

                                              (rt0 , td0 ) := MT0 .CommitfMT0 (iv ) .

          4. Set the prover index key pik := (ip , iv , td0 , ρ0 )
          5. Set the verifier index key vik := (rt0 , ρ0 ).
          6. Output (pik, vik).

Note that I is a deterministic algorithm, profiting from the benefits discussed in Remark 32.4.8.

The argument prover and verifier The argument prover P and argument verifier V are
constructed from the prover P and verifier V of the probabilistic proof. The construction
is similar to the relevant transformation in the non-preprocessing setting except for certain
differences.

  • P and V additionally receive as input pik = (ip , iv , td0 , ρ0 ) and vik = (rt0 , ρ0 ), respectively.
 3
     This step can be omitted in case the argument verifier does not need to hash the full instance (i, x), which
      is the case when constructing preprocessing interactive arguments (because, in such a case, the Fiat–Shamir
      transformation is not used). Specifically, this step can be omitted for the preprocessing extensions of the Kilian
      transformation and of the iBCS transformation. In this case, ρ0 is omitted from pik and vik.
32 Argument systems with preprocessing                                                         400




 • P additionally sends answers a0 to the queries Q0 of V to the verifier encoded index iv ,
   and a corresponding Merkle opening proof pf0 (computed from the trapdoor td0 and query
   set Q0 ) relative to the Merkle commitment rt0 .

 • V answers the queries Q0 of V to the verifier encoded index by using the answers a0
   received from the argument prover, and checks the validity of these query-answer pairs by
   using the Merkle commitment rt0 included in vik by I and the Merkle opening proof pf0
   received from P. Moreover, if relevant, V hashes the (short) pair (ρ0 , x) rather than the
   (long) full instance (i, x), which intuitively suffices since ρ0 is the hash of i included in vik
   by I.


32.4 Non-interactive arguments with preprocessing
Recall that a NARG in the ROM is a pair of oracle algorithms NARG = (P, V). In contrast, a
preprocessing NARG in the ROM is a triple of oracle algorithms

                                       PNARG = (I, P, V)

where I is the argument indexer, P is the argument prover, and V is the argument verifier. The
algorithm I is deterministic (in order to reduce the need to trust the offline phase as discussed
in Remark 32.4.8) and the algorithms P and V may be probabilistic.
   We discussed two settings for NARGs: the single-oracle setting in Chapters 4 and 5 and the
general-oracle setting in Chapter 7. The general-oracle setting extends the single-oracle setting
in that the NARG comes with an oracle distribution D that specifies the oracles used by the
NARG (see Definition 7.1.1). For the constructions studied in this book it is more convenient
to use the definitions for the general-oracle setting as the constructions rely on multiple oracles
of differing output lengths. Therefore, in this section we provide definitions for preprocessing
NARGs in the general-oracle setting. The single-oracle setting is directly implied from the
multiple-oracle setting, analogously to the case of (non-preprocessing) NARGs discussed in
Chapter 7.
   A preprocessing NARG with oracle distribution D works as follows. Given an index size
bound k and an instance size bound n, random oracles f are sampled from the distribution
D(λ, k, n). Anyone can query the oracles f , including the argument indexer I, the argument
prover P, and the argument verifier V.

 • Offline phase. The argument indexer I receives as input an index i, and outputs a prover
   index key pik and a verifier index key vik. The keys pik and vik can be used to prove and
   verify any number of statements involving the index i, with any instance x and witness w.

 • Online phase. The argument prover P receives as input the prover index key pik, an
   instance x, and a witness w, and outputs an argument string π. The argument verifier V
   receives as input the verifier index key vik, the instance x, and the argument string π, and
   outputs a bit denoting whether to accept (the bit is 1) or reject (the bit is 0).

See Figure 32.1a for a diagram of a preprocessing NARG.

Basic security definitions PNARG = (I, P, V) is a preprocessing NARG in the ROM for an
indexed relation Ri if it satisfies two main properties: (perfect) completeness and soundness.
32 Argument systems with preprocessing                                                     401




 • Completeness. Informally, for every index-instance-witness triple (i, x, w) P Ri , the
   argument indexer I on input i outputs a key pair (pik, vik) and the (honest) argument
   prover P on input (pik, x, w) outputs an argument string π such that the argument verifier
   V on input (vik, x, π) accepts, with probability 1. The probability here is taken over the
   choice of random oracle f , as well as any randomness of I, P, V.

 • Soundness. Informally, every malicious argument prover P̃ convinces the (honest)
   argument verifier V to accept an index-instance pair (i, x) R L(Ri ) with at most a small
   error probability that we denote by ARG (the probability is over the choice of random
   oracle f , as well as any randomness of P̃, V); the argument verifier V receives the verifier
   index key vik output by the argument indexer I rather than the index i itself.
    The malicious argument prover P̃ is computationally unbounded but may make at most
    t queries to the random oracle, for a given query bound t P N. In general, the error
    probability ARG depends on the query bound t, in addition to the security parameter λ.
    We consider the adaptive variant of soundness, capturing the case where the malicious
    argument prover P̃ chooses the index i and instance x adaptively after interacting with
    the random oracle. Hence ARG also depends on an index size bound k and an instance size
    bound n.

Below we provide the definitions of (perfect) completeness and (adaptive) soundness.

Definition 32.4.1. A preprocessing non-interactive argument PNARG = (I, P, V) for an
indexed relation Ri with oracle distribution D has (perfect) completeness if for every security
parameter λ P N, index size bound k P N, instance size bound n P N, and index-instance-witness
triple (i, x, w) P Ri with |i|Ri ď k and |x|Ri ď n,

Remark 32.4.8 (deterministic vs. probabilistic argument indexers). The definition of a
preprocessing NARG that we consider requires the argument indexer I to be a deterministic
algorithm. This is the case in many constructions of interest, including the construction that
we study in this chapter. Moreover, I being deterministic reduces the need for trust in the
preprocessing step: anyone can check that a given key pair (pik, vik) is the valid output of I f (i),
because they can rerun the computation and determine if the output matches the key pair.
  The more general case of a probabilistic argument indexer I is meaningful, but may demand
placing more trust in the preprocessing step. One option is to require I to be public-coin, which
means that all security properties of a preprocessing NARG hold even if the adversary knows
I’s randomness; in this case, I’s randomness can be published and, as in the deterministic
case, anyone can use that randomness to determine if a given key pair is the correct output.
However, if I is private-coin (its randomness must remain private) then the offline preprocessing
step must be carried out by a trusted party (or cryptographic replacements such as a secure
multi-party ceremony), which is undesirable.

Remark 32.4.9 (delegating the indexer computation). The argument indexer I performs a
deterministic computation to produce the index keys: (pik, vik) := I f (i). This computation
could itself be delegated to an untrusted argument prover in order to reduce the cost of
the trusted offline computation, for example, from poly(len(i)) to O(len(i)). In this case, the
untrusted argument prover would compute the index keys (pik, vik) and then prove the statement
32 Argument systems with preprocessing                                                           404




“(pik, vik) = I f (i)”, resulting in an argument string πi attesting to this statement. The security
properties of the preprocessing argument would then hold provided the tuple (i, pik, vik, πi )
satisfies the verification procedure of the delegation protocol (which should be cheaper than
the computation I f (i)). This notion of a preprocessing argument naturally arises, e.g., from
holographic IOPs wherein there is a public-coin IOP to verify the statement “(ip , iv ) := IHIOP (i)”.
We limit this remark to point the way to this relaxation without working out the details.


32.5 Holographic IOPs
Recall from Section 23.1 that an IOP is a pair of interactive algorithms IOP = (PIOP , VIOP ). In
contrast, a holographic IOP is a triple of algorithms

                                     HIOP = (IHIOP , PHIOP , VHIOP )

that works as follows. The IOP indexer receives as input an index i and outputs a prover
encoded index ip for the IOP prover and a verifier encoded index iv for the IOP verifier. The
IOP prover PHIOP receives as input the prover encoded index ip , instance x, and a witness w,
and the IOP verifier VHIOP receives query access to the verifier encoded index iv and receives as
input the instance x. They interact over some number k of rounds, where in each round i P [k]
the IOP prover PHIOP sends a proof string Πi and then the IOP verifier VHIOP sends a message
ρi . The IOP verifier may query any of the received proof strings at any location. After the
interaction, the IOP verifier VHIOP outputs a bit denoting whether to accept or reject, computed
based on the instance x, the IOP verifier’s own randomness, and the answers to any queries to
the verifier encoded index iv and to the proof strings (Πi )iP[k] (these form the entire view of
the IOP verifier). The IOP prover and the IOP verifier may be probabilistic, while the IOP
indexer is required to be deterministic (see Remark 32.5.10). See Figure 32.2d for a diagram of
a holographic IOP.
    The tuple HIOP = (IHIOP , PHIOP , VHIOP ) is an IOP for an indexed relation Ri with (perfect)
completeness and soundness error HIOP if it satisfies the two properties stated below.

Efficiency measures     We are interested in several efficiency measures of a holographic IOP.

  • Round complexity, denoted k, is the number of back-and-forth interactions between the
    IOP prover and IOP verifier. This excludes the IOP indexer in the offline phase.

  • Alphabets, denoted (Σi )ki=0 , are the alphabets used to write the verifier encoded index iv
    and proof strings (Πi )iP[k] .

  • Proof lengths, denoted (li )ki=0 , are the number of symbols in the verifier encoded index and
    each proof string. The verifier encoded index iv consists of l0 symbols; moreover,      for every
    i P [k], the i-th proof string Πi consists of li symbols. We define l := l0 + iP[k] li .
                                                                                   ř

  • Randomness sets, denoted (Ri )iP[k] , are the sets of randomness used by the IOP verifier in
    each round. For every i P [k], ř the i-th verifier message ρi is an element in Ri , consisting of
    log |Ri | bits. We define rtot := iP[k] log |Ri |.

  • Query complexities, denoted (qi )ki=0 , are the number of locations read by the verifier from
    the verifier encoded index and each proof string. The verifier reads q0 symbols from iv P Σl00 ;
                                                                                           li
                      ř i P [k], the verifier reads qi symbols from the proof string Πi P Σi . We
    moreover, for every
    define q := q0 + iP[k] qi .

  • Indexer time, prover time, and verifier time, denoted it, pt, vt, are the time complexities of
    the IOP indexer, of the IOP prover (to output the IOP strings), and of the IOP verifier
    (to output its decision bit).

The above efficiency measures may be functions of the index i and instance x (and possibly
other parameters associated to the construction of an IOP).

Remark 32.5.7. The IOP extractor EHIOP in Definitions 32.5.4 and 32.5.6 receives the index i
as input, so it can, if needed, recover the encoded indices ip and iv by running the (deterministic)
IOP indexer IHIOP (i), incurring the corresponding cost in time. One could relax either definition
by providing to EHIOP the encoded indices ip and iv as additional inputs.

Remark 32.5.10 (probabilistic IOP indexers). The definition of a holographic IOP that
we consider requires the IOP indexer IHIOP to be a deterministic algorithm. This is directly
motivated by the fact that in Section 32.4 the definition of a preprocessing NARG requires the
argument indexer I be a deterministic algorithm. In Remark 32.4.8 we explain how, while this
requirement helps reduce the need for trust in the offline phase, it is meaningful to consider
probabilistic relaxations for an argument indexer I. In light of that discussion, we note that:
(i) relaxing the definition of an argument indexer I to be a probabilistic public-coin algorithm
would directly motivate correspondingly relaxing the definition of an IOP indexer IHIOP to be a
probabilistic public-coin algorithm; and (ii) similarly for the case of a probabilistic private-coin
algorithm.


32.6 State restoration for holographic IOPs
We provide definitions for state-restoration soundness for public-coin holographic IOPs. These
definitions equal the definitions for public-coin IOPs in Section 23.2 except for minor syntactical
changes:
 • malicious IOP provers additionally output an index i, which then appears in relevant
   places (e.g., in a move of the state-restoration game, an input to the extractor, and so on);
   and

   The comparison between standard soundness and state-restoration soundness for public-coin
holographic IOPs is analogous to the case of IPs in Section 13.2.2. In particular, the security of
a non-interactive argument obtained from a given holographic IOP via the COS transformation
is characterized by the state-restoration soundness of the holographic IOP, as we discuss in
Section 32.8.2. Therefore, to ensure security of the COS transformation, one must assume that
the given holographic IOP has small state-restoration soundness error.
Remark 32.6.1. As for IOPs, small state-restoration soundness error for a holographic IOP is
implied by natural strong notions of soundness, such as special soundness (see Chapter 30) and
round-by-round soundness (see Chapter 31), appropriately modified to the holographic case.
We do not spell out these definitions and their implications to state-restoration soundness.

32.7 The COS transformation
The BCS transformation (Construction 25.1.1) maps a given (public-coin) IOP into a cor-
responding NARG in the ROM. Here we describe the COS transformation, which extends
the BCS transformation to map a given (public-coin) holographic IOP into a corresponding
preprocessing NARG in the ROM. The extension is intuitive, and could be equally applied to
any of the other transformations discussed in this book. We only spell out how to extend the
BCS transformation because this latter is the most general transformation (extending other
transformations is a special case); differences with the BCS transformation are colored in blue.
Construction 32.7.1. Let HIOP = (IHIOP , PHIOP , VHIOP ) be a public-coin holographic IOP with
round complexity k, proof lengths (li )ki=0 over alphabets (Σi )ki=0 , query complexities (qi )ki=0 ,
and verifier message sets (Ri )iP[k] . Let λ P N be a security parameter and sMT , sFS P N be
privacy parameters. Suppose that miniP[k] log |Ri | ě λ. Define MT0 := MT[λ, Σ0 , l0 , 0] and, for
every i P [k], MTi := MT[λ, Σi , li , sMT ] to be the Merkle commitment schemes with the stated
parameters; note that the privacy parameter in MT0 is set to 0 (no hiding is needed).
  We define PNARG := COS[IOP, (MTi )ki=0 , sFS ] to be the preprocessing non-interactive ar-
gument PNARG = (I, P, V) constructed as follows. The argument indexer receives as input
an index i; the argument prover P receives as input a prover index key pik, an instance
x, and witness w; the argument verifier V receives as input a verifier index key vik, the
instance x, and an argument string π. Both receive query access to 2 + 2k random oracles
f = (fMT0 , f0 , (fMTi )iP[k] , (fi )iP[k] ): (a) an oracle fMT0 P Ub (λ) used for the Merkle commitment
scheme MT0 , (b) an oracle f0 P Ub (λ) used to hash the index, (c) for every i P [k], an oracle
fMTi P Ub (λ) used for the Merkle commitment scheme MTi , and (d) for every i P [k], an
oracle fi P U(Ri ) used to derive IOP verifier randomness for round i (and extend                  the hash
chain). Hence the oracle distribution D is defined as D(λ, k, n) := Ub (λ)            2+k ¨ iP[k] U(Ri ) (see

Efficiency We discuss efficiency properties of the above construction, relative to the efficiency
of the BCS transformation.

 • Index keys. The prover index key pik has size O(len(ip ) + len(iv ) + λl0 ) and the verifier
   index key vik has size 2λ (in particular, vik is short).

 • Argument size. The argument string π in the above construction contains two parts: the
   tuple (Q0 , a0 , pf0 ) and a tuple that can be viewed as a BCS argument string πBCS (whose
   size is discussed in Equation 25.1). Hence, the additional size compared to the BCS
   transformation is
                                    O q0 ¨ log |Σ0 | + q0 ¨ λ ¨ log l0 .
                                                                      


 • Indexer complexity. The complexity of the argument indexer is typically dominated by the
   complexity of the underlying IOP indexer. Moreover, the number of queries to the random
   oracle is qI = O(l0 ); this is because the argument indexer hashes the index (one query)
   and commits to the verifier encoded index iv P Σl00 in O(l0 ) queries (via MT0 .Commit).

 • Prover complexity. The complexity of the argument prover is similar to that in the BCS
   transformation. The additional cost in computation and queries are second-order
                                                                                 ř terms.
   In particular, the number of queries to the random oracle remains qP = O(k + iP[k] li ).

 • Verifier complexity. The complexity of the argument verifier is similar to that in the BCS
   transformation. The additional cost in computation and queries are second-order   terms. In
   particular, the number of queries to the random oracle remains qV = O(k + iP[k] qi ¨ log li ).

32.8 Security of the COS transformation
The COS transformation is an extension of the BCS transformation, so security properties
of the COS transformation can, in general, be proved via similar approaches as for the BCS
transformation. Intuitively, the soundness error and knowledge soundness error of the COS
transformation incur a small additive error over the respective errors of the BCS transformation,
quantifying the security of the offline phase; in contrast, the zero-knowledge error of the COS
transformation is the same as that of the BCS transformation because the security of the offline
phase does not affect the zero knowledge property.

Organization In Section 32.8.1 we describe a security reduction from the COS transformation
to the BCS transformation: we show how a malicious argument prover against the COS verifier
can be transformed into a corresponding malicious argument prover against the BCS verifier, up
to a small additive error that quantifies the security of the offline phase. This reduction allows
us to prove in Section 32.8.2 the soundness and in Section 32.8.3 the knowledge soundness

32.8.1 From COS to BCS
We provide a security reduction from the COS transformation to the BCS transformation,
by describing how a malicious argument prover against the COS verifier can be reduced to a
corresponding malicious argument prover against the BCS verifier, quantifying the security loss
of this reduction.

From HIOP to IOP We describe how to “downcast” a given holographic IOP into a cor-
responding (non-holographic) IOP wherein the honest prover and honest verifier each take
responsibility of the offline phase. The transformation is conceptually simple, though demands
some text to state precisely due to the different settings.

Definition 32.8.1. Given an indexed relation Ri , the corresponding (non-indexed) relation is

                                  R(Ri ) := t((i, x), w) : (i, x, w) P Ri u .

Construction 32.8.2. Let HIOP = (IHIOP , PHIOP , VHIOP ) be a holographic IOP for an indexed
relation Ri . We define a (standard) IOP IOP = (PIOP , VIOP ) for the relation R(Ri ).

  • The IOP prover PIOP receives as input a full instance (i, x) and a witness w, computes
    the encoded indices (ip , iv ) := IHIOP (i), and then emulates the HIOP prover PHIOP on input
    (ip , x, w).

  • The IOP verifier VIOP receives as input a full instance (i, x), computes the encoded indices
    (ip , iv ) := IHIOP (i), and then emulates the HIOP verifier VHIOP given query access to iv and
    input x.

   The non-holographic IOP IOP derived from the holographic IOP HIOP differs in computational
efficiency but is otherwise “equivalent” from the perspective of security, as in the following
lemma.

From COS to BCS The preprocessing NARG whose security we wish to analyze is obtained
by applying the COS transformation to the holographic IOP HIOP. We compare this to the
(non-preprocessing) NARG obtained by applying the BCS transformation to the corresponding
(non-holographic) IOP IOP from Construction 32.8.2. We define these two NARGs below:

                              (ICOS , PCOS , VCOS ) := COS[IOP, (MTi )ki=0 , sFS ] ,
                                    (PBCS , VBCS ) := BCS[IOP, (MTi )iP[k] , sFS ] .

Construction 32.8.4 explains how to transform a malicious argument prover P̃COS against
VCOS into a malicious argument prover P̃BCS ( P̃COS ) against VBCS . Then Construction 32.8.5
describes an algorithm COSToBCSTrace that transforms the query-answer trace of P̃COS into
the query-answer trace of P̃BCS ( P̃COS ).

Construction 32.8.5. The function COSToBCSTrace                      śreceives as input a query-answer trace
tr for oracles (fMT0 , f0 , (fMTi )iP[k] , (fi )iP[k] ) P Ub (λ)2+k ¨ iP[k] U(Ri ) and outputs a query-answer

                                                                  ś

      COSToBCSTrace(tr):
       1. Initialize an empty list of move-response pairs trBCS .
       2. For each query-answer (x, y) in tr (taken in order):
            – if x is a query to fMT0 , then do nothing;
            – if x is a query to f0 , then do nothing;
            – if x is a query to fMTi , append (x, y) to trBCS as a query to fMTi ;
            – if x is a query to fi with i P t2, . . . , ku, append (x, y) to trBCS as a query to fi ;
            – if x is a query to f1 then:
                 a) parse x as a tuple (ρ0 , x, rt1 , τ1 ) (if not possible then do nothing);
                 b) search for all prior queries to f0 whose answer is ρ0 ;
                 c) if a unique such query x0 is found then append (((x0 , x), rt1 , τ1 ), x0 ) to trBCS
                     as a query to f1 ;
                 d) if no such queries or more than one such query is found then do nothing.
       3. Output trBCS .

The running time of COSToBCSTrace is O(rmax ¨ t + tFS ¨ λ ¨ log t0 + λ ¨ t0 ¨ log t0 ), where the term
O(rmax ¨ t) comes from a linear pass on the queries and the term O(tFS ¨ λ ¨ log t0 + λ ¨ t0 ¨ log t0 )
comes from processing queries to f1 (as explained in the last paragraph of Construction 32.8.4).

argument prover P̃COS against VCOS into the malicious argument prover P̃BCS ( P̃COS ) against VBCS .
